Structure this in three parts under 90 seconds: a one-line professional summary (years of experience, core specialization), a brief walk through career progression highlighting the roles/achievements most relevant to this job, and a closing line connecting your background to why this specific opportunity interests you - avoid reciting your full resume chronologically.
You have around 7 years of experience, r: Confirm your actual years directly and precisely rather than rounding - if the interviewer's number is off, correct it politely and clearly, since experience-level mismatches affect how the rest of the interview is calibrated.
Have you worked on GCP, AWS, and Azure?: Answer with honest per-cloud depth rather than a blanket yes - e.g. 'primarily GCP day-to-day, working AWS knowledge from a past project, limited hands-on Azure' - since a vague 'yes to all three' invites deep follow-ups on whichever cloud you're weakest in.
Have you worked on on-prem servers or on: Answer honestly with specifics - if on-prem experience exists, mention what (bare metal, VMware, physical networking) since on-prem experience signals deeper fundamentals (you can't rely on managed services abstracting problems away); if cloud-only, that's fine to state plainly too.
Have you worked on EKS?: Answer with actual scope - cluster count, whether you managed cluster creation/upgrades or only deployed workloads onto an existing cluster, and one concrete example of an issue you resolved on EKS specifically (which can differ operationally from GKE in areas like IAM-to-Kubernetes-RBAC mapping and networking).
Have you launched an EKS cluster?: Answer honestly, and if yes, be ready to describe the method (eksctl, Terraform, or the AWS console/CloudFormation), the node group configuration (managed vs. self-managed, instance types), and any networking decisions (VPC CNI configuration, public/private subnets) made during setup.
Did you create the EKS cluster using Ter: State the actual method used and why - Terraform is generally preferred for consistency with the rest of infrastructure-as-code and easier multi-environment replication; eksctl/CloudFormation are faster for a one-off or AWS-native-only setup; manual console creation is reasonable to admit for early learning/POC work but should be qualified as such.
Suppose an application is down. How will: Start with impact/scope (all users or some, one region or all), check the service's health dashboard/SLO status, correlate with recent changes (deploys, config changes, infra changes) in the timeframe the outage started, then narrow into logs/traces for the specific failing component - mitigate (rollback, scale, failover) before fully root-causing if impact is severe.
What is the difference between ADD and C: `COPY` simply copies files/directories from the build context into the image, nothing more. `ADD` does everything COPY does plus two extra behaviors: it can auto-extract local tar archives into the destination, and it can fetch a remote URL directly into the image. Because ADD's extra behaviors are often surprising/implicit, `COPY` is the recommended default unless you specifically need ADD's archive-extraction behavior.
What is the difference between docker bu: `docker build` creates an image reproducibly from a Dockerfile - the recommended way, since the build steps are version-controlled and repeatable. `docker commit` snapshots a running container's current filesystem state into a new image - useful for quick debugging/experimentation, but not reproducible or reviewable, so it's not used for building production images.
How can you minimize the Docker image si: Use a minimal base image (alpine, distroless, or slim variants), use multi-stage builds so build tools/dependencies never reach the final image, combine RUN commands to reduce layer count and clean up package manager caches within the same layer they were created (not a later layer, since earlier layers remain in the image regardless), and use `.dockerignore` to avoid copying unnecessary files into the build context.
What is a Headless Service?: A Service with `clusterIP: None` - instead of load-balancing through a single virtual IP, DNS lookups for a headless Service return the IPs of all matching Pods directly, letting clients discover and connect to individual Pods themselves. This is commonly used for StatefulSets, where each Pod replica needs a stable, individually addressable identity (e.g. connecting to a specific database replica) rather than being load-balanced anonymously.
What is the default NodePort range?: 30000-32767 by default in Kubernetes - when a Service of type NodePort is created without an explicit port specified, Kubernetes allocates a port from within this range on every node, which can be customized cluster-wide via the API server's `--service-node-port-range` flag if needed.
If NodePort gives only a port, how do yo: Use any worker node's IP combined with the allocated NodePort (`http://<any-node-ip>:<nodeport>`) - traffic to that port on any node gets routed to the Service regardless of which node the actual Pod is running on, since kube-proxy sets up forwarding rules on every node for every NodePort Service.
If there are 10-20 worker nodes, which n: Any of them work identically since NodePort routes traffic from any node to the correct Pod - in practice, though, relying on one specific node's IP is fragile (that node could be drained/removed), so production setups front NodePort with a proper external Load Balancer distributing across all node IPs, rather than hardcoding a single node's address anywhere.
If the Load Balancer is down, how will y: As a workaround, bypass the Load Balancer entirely and hit the application directly via `<any-node-ip>:<nodeport>` to confirm whether the application itself is healthy (isolating whether the issue is the LB or the app), then troubleshoot the Load Balancer itself separately (health check configuration, backend registration, LB service quotas/logs) since NodePort access confirms the app tier is fine and narrows the problem to the LB layer specifically.
How do you expose a service outside the: A Service of type LoadBalancer (provisions a cloud load balancer automatically) for simple single-service exposure, or an Ingress resource behind an Ingress Controller for HTTP(S) traffic needing host/path-based routing across many services through one external entry point - Ingress is generally preferred at any meaningful scale since provisioning a separate cloud load balancer per service (via LoadBalancer type) gets expensive and harder to manage.
Which Ingress Controller are you using?: Answer with the actual controller (NGINX Ingress, GKE's native Ingress/Gateway, Traefik) and one concrete configuration detail (TLS termination setup, path-based routing rules configured) to demonstrate real hands-on use rather than just naming it.
How do you install or setup the NGINX In: Typically via Helm: `helm install ingress-nginx ingress-nginx/ingress-nginx -n ingress-nginx --create-namespace` - this deploys the controller Pods plus a Service (usually type LoadBalancer, which provisions a GCP external load balancer automatically) that becomes the actual entry point Ingress resources route through.
You already have a GKE cluster. How will: Install the controller (via Helm, as above) into the existing cluster, then create Ingress resources referencing the controller via its `ingressClassName`, defining host/path rules pointing to backend Services - the controller watches for Ingress resources and configures its underlying proxy (nginx config) to match automatically.
Why do we use an Ingress Controller?: It provides a single, cost-efficient external entry point that can route to many backend Services based on hostname/path, handle TLS termination centrally, and apply cross-cutting concerns (rate limiting, auth, rewrites) consistently - versus provisioning a separate cloud load balancer per Service (via type LoadBalancer), which is far more expensive and harder to manage at scale.
If NGINX Ingress is deprecated, what wil: The Kubernetes Gateway API is the forward-looking replacement for the older Ingress API, offering a more expressive, role-oriented model (separating infrastructure/platform concerns from route definitions) - GKE Gateway Controller and other Gateway API implementations are the migration path being adopted as Ingress-based controllers age out.
How will you expose applications after m: Migrate Ingress resources to Gateway API resources (Gateway + HTTPRoute), which express the same host/path routing and TLS termination concepts in a newer, more extensible API - most cloud providers and major ingress controllers now support the Gateway API as either a direct replacement or alongside their existing Ingress support during a transition period.
How do you expose an application using a: Define a Service manifest with a selector matching the target Pods' labels, specify the port/targetPort mapping, and choose the appropriate type (ClusterIP for internal-only, NodePort/LoadBalancer for external access) - `kubectl apply -f service.yaml` creates it, and `kubectl get svc` confirms the assigned virtual IP/external IP.
Why do we use Namespaces?: Namespaces provide logical isolation within a single cluster - scoping resource names (the same name can exist in different namespaces without conflict), enabling per-team/per-environment RBAC and ResourceQuotas, and giving a clean boundary for organizing resources by team, environment, or application without needing separate clusters for each.
What is the role of etcd?: etcd is Kubernetes' backing store - a distributed, consistent key-value store holding the entire cluster state (every object's spec and status). The API server is the only component that talks to etcd directly; everything else (scheduler, controllers, kubelets) reads/writes cluster state exclusively through the API server, which persists it to etcd.
Can you take a backup of etcd?: Yes - `etcdctl snapshot save <path>` creates a point-in-time snapshot of etcd's data, which can be restored (`etcdctl snapshot restore`) to recover the entire cluster's state in a disaster recovery scenario. On managed Kubernetes (GKE, EKS), the cloud provider handles etcd backup/HA for you as part of the managed control plane.
How does the kube-apiserver communicate: The API server communicates with etcd over gRPC (etcd's native client protocol), typically secured with mutual TLS, and is the sole component with direct etcd access - all reads and writes to cluster state go through this single path, which is what keeps etcd's data model consistent and lets Kubernetes enforce validation/admission control uniformly before anything is persisted.
What is a DaemonSet?: A DaemonSet ensures exactly one copy of a Pod runs on every node (or a selected subset via node selectors/affinity) in the cluster, automatically adding a Pod to any new node that joins and removing it when a node leaves - used for node-level agents like log collectors, monitoring exporters, or CNI/storage plugins that need to run everywhere.
How does the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (: HPA periodically checks a workload's current metric value (CPU/memory via metrics-server, or custom metrics via an adapter) against a target, and adjusts the replica count proportionally to close the gap - e.g. if average CPU is at 150% of target, HPA roughly increases replicas by that ratio, subject to configured min/max bounds and a stabilization window to avoid rapid flapping.
Does HPA scale based on resource request: Resource requests - HPA computes utilization as actual usage divided by the requested amount, not the limit, which is why every workload using HPA must have resource requests explicitly set; without them, HPA has no baseline to calculate a meaningful utilization percentage from.
Explain StorageClass, Persistent Volume: A StorageClass defines a 'class' of storage (e.g. SSD vs. standard disk) and the provisioner that creates volumes dynamically on demand. A PersistentVolume represents actual provisioned storage in the cluster. A PersistentVolumeClaim is a Pod's request for storage (size, access mode) - when a PVC references a StorageClass, Kubernetes dynamically provisions a matching PV automatically rather than requiring one to be pre-created manually.
What is the difference between static pr: Static provisioning requires an administrator to manually create PersistentVolumes ahead of time, which PVCs then bind to. Dynamic provisioning (via a StorageClass) creates the underlying storage automatically at the moment a PVC is created, with no manual pre-creation step - dynamic provisioning is the standard approach in cloud environments since it removes that manual bottleneck entirely.
How do you take a backup of your Kuberne: Use a dedicated backup tool like Velero, which backs up both Kubernetes object state (via the API server) and persistent volume data (via cloud snapshot integration or restic), enabling full cluster or namespace-level restore - relying on etcd snapshots alone backs up object definitions but not the actual data inside persistent volumes.
What is the difference between volume an: `volumes` (at the Pod spec level) declares the actual storage source available to the Pod (an emptyDir, a PVC, a ConfigMap, etc.). `volumeMounts` (at the container level) specifies where inside that specific container's filesystem a declared volume should be mounted - one Pod-level volume can be mounted at different paths in multiple containers within the same Pod.
What kind of Jenkins pipelines have you: Describe with specifics - declarative multibranch pipelines for CI (build/test/scan per PR), deployment pipelines with manual approval gates for production, and any Shared Library work for reusable stages across teams - naming actual pipeline purposes rather than a generic 'CI/CD pipelines' claim.
How do you take a backup of Jenkins?: Back up the Jenkins home directory (`JENKINS_HOME`), which contains job configurations, plugin data, build history, and credentials - either via a scheduled filesystem/volume snapshot if Jenkins runs on a persistent disk, or using a dedicated backup plugin (ThinBackup) that handles this on a schedule with retention, ideally storing backups off the Jenkins host itself.
Have you used Argo CD or Harness?: Answer with actual scope for whichever tool - Applications/pipelines you've configured, whether you set up the tool itself or just used an existing setup, and one concrete example (a sync issue debugged, a deployment pipeline built) to substantiate real hands-on experience.
How does Argo CD work?: ArgoCD continuously compares the desired state declared in a Git repository against the live state of a Kubernetes cluster, and either automatically or on-demand syncs (applies) any difference to make the cluster match Git - this reconciliation loop is what makes deployments Git-driven (a merge triggers a sync) rather than requiring someone to manually run kubectl/Helm commands.
If someone changes a Kubernetes resource: ArgoCD detects the live cluster state now differs from what's declared in Git (shown as 'OutOfSync'), and if auto-sync with self-heal is enabled, it automatically reverts the manual change back to match Git on the next reconciliation - this is by design, since Git is meant to be the single source of truth, and any out-of-band change is treated as drift to be corrected.
Explain the ELK Stack along with OpenTel: ELK (Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana - often Filebeat replaces Logstash for lighter shipping) is a log aggregation and search/visualization stack: logs are collected, indexed in Elasticsearch, and explored via Kibana dashboards. OpenTelemetry is a separate, broader standard for generating and exporting metrics/logs/traces from instrumented applications - in a combined setup, OpenTelemetry's Collector can receive telemetry and export logs specifically into the ELK stack (or traces into Elasticsearch's APM support), unifying instrumentation with ELK's storage/visualization.
What is the complete log flow from the a: Application writes logs (ideally structured JSON) to stdout/a file -> a log shipper (Filebeat, Fluentd, or an OpenTelemetry Collector) on the node/sidecar picks them up and forwards them -> Logstash (optional, for transformation/enrichment) or directly to Elasticsearch for indexing -> Kibana queries Elasticsearch to render dashboards and enable search across the indexed logs.
What is the role of the OpenTelemetry Co: The Collector receives telemetry data (metrics, logs, traces) from instrumented applications via various protocols, processes it (batching, filtering, adding metadata), and exports it to one or more configured backends (Prometheus, Elasticsearch, Jaeger) - it decouples applications from needing to know exactly where telemetry ultimately goes, since that's configured centrally in the Collector rather than in every application.
What is the role of the APM Server?: Elastic's APM Server receives application performance monitoring data (traces, transaction timings, errors) from APM agents instrumented in application code, and indexes it into Elasticsearch in a schema Kibana's APM UI understands - giving visibility into transaction latency breakdowns and error rates correlated with the same logs already in Elasticsearch.
How do you delete old logs from Elastics: Configure Index Lifecycle Management (ILM) policies that automatically roll over indices at a size/age threshold and delete indices past a defined retention period - this is the standard automated approach rather than manually running delete-by-query, which doesn't scale and is easy to forget to run consistently.
If ILM is not working and Elasticsearch: As an immediate fix, manually delete the oldest indices directly (`DELETE /<old-index-name>`) to free disk space and restore cluster health (a full disk can put Elasticsearch into a read-only state), then investigate why ILM isn't executing (check the ILM policy is actually attached to the index template, and check ILM's own status/errors via `GET _ilm/status` and per-index `explain` calls) so the automated cleanup resumes working going forward.
If Kibana is not working, how will you t: Check Kibana's own logs first for startup/connection errors, confirm it can actually reach Elasticsearch (a common cause - Elasticsearch being down, unreachable, or a version mismatch between Kibana and Elasticsearch), check Kibana's resource usage (memory/CPU) for exhaustion, and confirm the Kibana service/Pod itself is actually running and healthy before assuming the issue is data/query related.
If a Linux server has very high load, ho: Identify what's actually driving load first (`top`/`htop` to see whether it's CPU-bound processes, or `iostat`/`vmstat` if it's I/O wait inflating load average) - then act accordingly: kill/throttle a runaway process, scale the workload to another instance, or address the actual I/O/resource bottleneck rather than assuming high load always means 'add more CPU.'
How do you check whether an application: `ps aux | grep <process>` or `systemctl status <service>` to confirm the process/service is alive, `netstat -tlnp` or `ss -tlnp` to confirm it's actually listening on its expected port, and a direct `curl` to its health endpoint to confirm it's not just running but actually responding correctly.
If you cannot log in to the server, how: Use the cloud provider's monitoring dashboard (CPU/memory/network graphs from outside the box) if SSH itself is unreachable, or the serial/console output for a lower-level view - both let you assess whether the server is overloaded/unresponsive without needing an interactive shell session on it.
Have you worked on GKE or GCE?: Answer with actual scope for each - operational depth on GKE (cluster/node pool management vs. just deploying workloads) and GCE (VM provisioning, image management, autoscaling groups) - naming concrete examples for whichever you have deeper experience with.
Which GCP services have you worked on?: List by category with honest depth noted for each - Compute (GKE, Compute Engine), Storage (Cloud Storage, Persistent Disk), Networking (VPC, Cloud Load Balancing), Data (BigQuery, Cloud SQL), and Operations (Cloud Monitoring/Logging) - rather than a flat list implying equal expertise across all of them.
Which monitoring tools have you worked o: List with the actual role each played in your stack - metrics collection (Prometheus, Cloud Monitoring), visualization (Grafana), and alerting (Alertmanager, PagerDuty) - since interviewers are gauging whether you understand how these fit together, not just tool familiarity in isolation.
Have you worked on Prometheus and Grafan: Answer with actual scope - whether you deployed/operated Prometheus itself (scrape configs, retention, alerting rules) or primarily viewed dashboards someone else built, and whether you've written PromQL queries yourself versus just consuming pre-built Grafana dashboards.
Did you integrate Prometheus and Grafana: If yes, describe the actual integration - adding Prometheus as a Grafana data source, building or importing dashboards, and configuring any alerting rules - with one concrete dashboard/alert example to substantiate real hands-on setup work rather than just using an existing pre-integrated stack.
Have you worked with Helm?: Answer with actual scope - authoring charts from scratch versus consuming/customizing existing public charts by overriding values, and one concrete example (which chart, what it deployed, how you organized values per environment).
How did you deploy Sentinel Antivirus us: Describe the deployment as a DaemonSet-based Helm chart (since antivirus/EDR agents typically need to run on every node), configuring values for the specific environment (API keys/tenant config via Secrets, resource requests/limits sized for the agent's footprint), and installing via `helm install`/`upgrade` through the same CI/CD or manual process used for other cluster-wide agents.
Was Sentinel deployed as a container?: Yes - security/antivirus agents like Sentinel are typically packaged as containers and deployed via a DaemonSet so the agent runs alongside workloads on every node, giving it the node-level visibility it needs to monitor for threats across all containers running there.
Was Sentinel deployed on all worker node: Typically yes, via a DaemonSet (which by default schedules a Pod on every node) - unless specific nodes were deliberately excluded via taints/node selectors (e.g. a specialized node pool where the agent isn't needed or isn't compatible), the standard pattern for a security agent is cluster-wide coverage so no node is left unmonitored.
